If you have concerns about exam and assessment activities in your school or college, or at an awarding organisation, contact the awarding organisation, and then if necessary contact Ofqual.

What to tell your students

Remind students of the exam rules and that malpractice can lead to serious consequences, including disqualification.

What schools and colleges must do to prevent malpractice and maladministration in exams and assessments

Schools and colleges are responsible for preventing malpractice and maladministration, investigating allegations, and following awarding organisations’ rules for conducting exams. This is a very important role.

Breaking rules can make assessments unfair and put the value of a qualification at risk.

Awarding organisations rightly expect you to take malpractice and maladministration, and the risk of them, seriously. They expect you to have processes for investigating and dealing with allegations. Awarding organisations have their own rules for when and how exams and other assessments are conducted, which you must follow.

What you should do

Take malpractice and maladministration, and the risk of them, seriously. Don’t assume it couldn’t happen at your school or college.

Have processes for investigating and dealing with allegations of malpractice or maladministration.

Follow awarding organisations’ rules for when and how exams and other assessments are conducted.

Comply with awarding organisations’ instructions to reduce the risk of errors and maladministration, such as having 2 people present when opening exam papers.

Follow instructions about issuing results. For example, you must not give results to students before any embargo is lifted.

What to tell your students

Breaking the rules can result in students’ assessed work being rejected, action being taken against the school or college, or both.

Committing malpractice could mean students are not awarded grades – and not just for the qualification the rule breaking relates to. Grades for other exams could be withheld too, including by other awarding organisations.

How to report malpractice or maladministration in exams or assessments

You should report any evidence or suspicions of malpractice to the relevant awarding organisation. You should report any errors or incidents of maladministration as soon as they are discovered.

Individuals can also report concerns to Ofqual under the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998. This is often known as whistleblowing. In certain circumstances, this can provide protection when a person discloses concerns about practice where they work.

Our complaints procedure page gives details of how to report suspected malpractice or wrongdoing to Ofqual.

What you should do

Report any evidence or suspicions of malpractice or maladministration to the relevant awarding organisation as soon as possible.

Individuals can report concerns to Ofqual as a whistleblower.

Awarding organisation inspections

Awarding organisations, sometimes through JCQ’s Centre Inspection Service, may carry out visits to check that you are following exam requirements correctly.

Ofqual requires awarding organisations to have a sanctions policy for when a school or college has breached its requirements. Sanctions include extra monitoring visits, use of awarding organisation invigilators or preventing a school or college from offering some or all of its qualifications.

JCQ publishes guidance setting out how exam boards investigate potential malpractice and the sanctions they may impose when malpractice is confirmed. Awarding organisations offering VTQs will have their own policies that cover inspection, investigation, and sanctions.

Ofqual will not normally be involved with the investigation. Where you think an awarding organisation has not followed published procedures, you can appeal against the finding. If you are dissatisfied with the awarding organisation’s response, you can complain to Ofqual. We will usually only consider a complaint once the awarding organisation’s own complaints and appeals procedures have been exhausted.

What you should do

If you think an awarding organisation has not followed its inspections procedures correctly, you can appeal against the finding. If you are dissatisfied with the response, you can complain to Ofqual.

How to report a concern about exams as a whistleblower

Whistleblowing to Ofqual is one way a member of staff in a school or college can raise a concern about wrongdoing, risk or malpractice in their workplace.

A protected disclosure under whistleblowing law means reporting a genuine concern about wrongdoing. It should not be about a personal grievance. When whistleblowing to Ofqual it would typically need to relate to exams, assessments, qualifications or the organisations that award them.

You can find more information on whistleblowing in Ofqual’s whistleblowing policy.

What you should do

Read Ofqual’s whistleblowing policy if you feel you may need to report a concern and follow the steps outlined in the policy.

More information about Ofqual, contact details and useful links

Ofqual regulates awarding organisations that design, deliver and award qualifications and assessments in England. We control entry to the regulated market and have rules and guidance for awarding organisations to make sure regulated qualifications are fit for purpose, valid and delivered securely.

Ofqual’s Understanding grading toolkit is designed to help headteachers and teachers understand and explain how GCSE and A Level qualifications are marked and graded.

Ofqual’s YouTube channel features video resources to help you understand exams, qualifications and assessments in England.

Can I Just Qualify That? is Ofqual’s podcast for teachers.

Ofqual has resources to support exams officers in their roles.
